Practical experience has shown that on-farm scheduling can be approximated by measuring the water use from a wash tub. However, the irrigation requirement for alfalfa is governed by rainfall and the water holding capacity of the soils growing the crop. results.title: Effect of drought on alfalfa and managing for the next growing season – Crops and Soils
results.description:
Drought can significantly reduce alfalfa yield. Timing of drought can be critical. First cutting may be reduced in the case of a dry March. Alfalfa root systems die back to some extent over winter. The root system requires good soil moisture in the early spring to regrow. If a strong root system forms then high yields will occur on first cutting. If the root system growth is restricted by dry soil, then the top growth will be reduced, even if good rain occurs in the later part of the first [...] Cell enlargement is inhibited.
 The number of basal buds and the number of shoots or stems/plant is reduced when moisture stress occurs in the first 14 days after a harvest.
 The stem internode length is reduced; thus, the flowering is seen at reduced plant height.
 Leaf area/leaf size and leaf growth rate is reduced, although to a lesser degree than stem growth. Therefore, leaf to stem ratio is higher under moisture stress. [...] If stand is over 10 inches tall and flowering, harvest if economic to do so. Moisture stressed alfalfa should be mowed at the normal cutting height. requirements.missing: No supplied document provides a university or peer-reviewed decision rule specifying when to resume alfalfa irrigation after rainfall. Documents cover general soil-moisture thresholds (s11, s14), visual stress indicators (s11), and calendar/ET-based scheduling (s10, s11, s12), but none address the post-rainfall restart decision—e.g., whether to wait for ET depletion, what soil-water deficit percentage or matric potential triggers re-irrigation after rain, or a documented field indicator tied to a quantitative threshold.

No supplied document reports a post-rainfall irrigation-resume threshold with explicit units and clear field-alfalfa scope. s11 provides matric-potential ranges by soil texture (e.g., sand 40–50 kPa, clay loam 100–120 kPa) and s14 gives AWC tables for Minnesota soils, but these are general irrigation-scheduling references, not thresholds tied to the specific question of when to restart irrigation after rainfall. No document states a % available-water-depletion or mm-depth trigger applicable after a rain event for field-grown alfalfa at a defined growth stage or geography.
